title: The refusal event payload cannot be built from the refusal the tree actually throws
description:
Found in review of fiddlybits-52v.6.8 after it merged at acc31ad.

Decision 0042 gives the refusal event the payload 'the component, what was refused, the quantity and the bound it violated', and src/Events/Events.jl reads that as RefusalPayload(component::String, refused::String, quantity::Float64, bound::Float64). Every refusal the tree raises is Verdicts.refuse(quantity, site, reason), which carries three strings and no number at all, and Verdicts.Refusal is the type every module above Verdicts throws.

So there is no path from a raised refusal to a refusal event. fiddlybits-52v.6.7 installs the journal sink and will have to write these, and at that point it has a Refusal in hand carrying a quantity NAME where the payload wants a quantity VALUE, a reason sentence with nowhere to go, and a bound that was never recorded. Two records for one concept, which is the two-definitions failure the one-definition rule names.

The judgement is which record is right, and it is a judgement rather than a transcription, which is why this is frontier rather than sonnet. Either the payload's quantity and bound are the numbers 0042 reads as, and Verdicts.Refusal gains them so a refusal carries what it violated, or the payload is the three strings the tree already raises and 0042's line is read the other way. Whichever way it goes, one of the two records changes and the decision record says which and why.

title: Events ties no payload shape to a kind, and drops an unrecognised keyword without a word
description:
Found in review of fiddlybits-52v.6.8 after it merged at acc31ad. Two holes in src/Events/Events.jl, both measured on the merged tree.

Event carries payload::Any and its constructor takes any kind beside any payload, so Event(Verdict(), 1, 0.0, :fast, "Mesh", BudgetPayload(cap=1.0, which="mem")) constructs a verdict event carrying a budget payload. Decision 0042 says every event has the same header and a payload whose shape is FIXED PER KIND, and the provenance plan repeats it: a reader filters on the header without knowing any payload, and a query written against one kind keeps working when another is added. Neither holds while any kind may carry any payload. The fix is a declared payload_type per kind and a constructor that refuses the mismatch, which also makes the pairing something the enumeration test can walk.

build_payload collects its keywords into a Dict and reads only the fields of T out of it, so a keyword that is not a field is dropped in silence. VerdictPayload(predicate="L", verdict=Converged(), statistic=0.5, bracket=(0.0,1.0), typo=99) constructs and returns a payload with no sign that typo was given. A misspelled field is then an event written with a default nobody asked for, which is what the no-silent-default rule exists against; the missing-field half already refuses correctly and this is its other side.

Neither was in fiddlybits-52v.6.8's acceptance, which is why the row merged rather than widening.

title: Geometry allocates a heap vector for every cross, normalize and broadcast; carry a cell's vertices in SVectors
description:
Raised in review of fiddlybits-52v.2.3 after it merged at 3062db1. A @view avoids copying a matrix column, but arithmetic, cross and normalize over an AbstractVector allocate a new heap array for the result, and geometry does that dozens of times per cell: the circumcentre, three midpoints, six sub-triangle areas, two edge tangents and the normal.

Measured on yggdrasil, Julia 1.12.7, best of three with a collection between runs:

  level 5   0.0177 s    49.8 MiB allocated, output 2.6 MiB
  level 6   0.0694 s   199.1 MiB allocated, output 10.3 MiB
  level 7   0.3349 s   796.3 MiB allocated, output 41.3 MiB

Loading each cell's three vertices, and each edge's two vertices and two circumcentres, into SVector{3,Float64} at the top of the loops keeps every subsequent operation in registers. The mathematical notation is unchanged, and the helper signatures already take AbstractVector so they accept an SVector unchanged.

title: The dual area sum, the primal-to-dual right angle and the circumcentre spread have no registered threshold; measure their floors and carry them
description:
Found in frontier review of fiddlybits-52v.2.3. REQ-TER-011 requires both area sums to close and names the primal-to-dual edge angle as a tested property, but docs/oracles/registry.toml states mesh.area_closure over the primal sum alone, and the finding behind it measured only the primal cell area. Three quantities the geometry row has to judge therefore have no threshold to judge against.

The dual sum is not the primal sum. Each dual cell is assembled from sub-triangles, six per primal cell, so its floor is six times the primal's by the registry's own derivation, per-piece floor times piece count. At level 0 the dual sum lands outside the primal's N eps bar and inside 6N eps.

The primal-to-dual right angle and the circumcentre's equidistance from its cell's three vertices are not level-independent the way an area is. The stored vertex coordinates carry an absolute rounding, so a triangle of edge h carries a relative rounding of eps over h in every difference the circumcentre is built from, and the floor doubles with each level rather than staying flat.

Without this row the geometry row would either invent a flat bar or, as its first pass did, compute the dual area as a remainder against the primal so that the dual closure could not fail.

title: Events: the closed journal vocabulary, typed payloads, and the one front door with a no-op sink
description:
Found in the plan review: the kernels plan, the coupling plan and the mesh plan each declared their own hook for something Provenance fills, which is three definitions of one mechanism. Every module that emits a journal event or records a device move sits below Provenance in the include order, so the front door has to be declared low and once.

Events is a group A submodule referencing only Verdicts. It declares the ten event kinds of decision 0042 as singleton types enumerated by kinds() and closed by a subtype check, the typed payload struct per kind, the common header, emit(event) which hands the event to an installed sink, sink!(f) which installs one, and moved(array, from, to) for the device-move record of decision 0010. The default sink is a no-op, which is what the journal's inertness requires. Provenance's journal.jl is the only sink ever installed and the lint protects its path constant.

title: FixedPointLoop, Ladder and the finalizer that verifies rather than iterates
description:
FixedPointLoop carries a body, an exit predicate over the history, a declared monotonicity, an iteration cap and a run floor decided before the loop starts. Ladder holds the loops and a finalizer. An exit predicate returns one of the five LoopVerdict values from Verdicts, never a boolean and never a number.

A loop declared Antitone cannot return Converged: its exit is a bracket by construction, and its Bracketed verdict reports the width and the overshoot separately, because a bracket whose overshoot is hidden inside its width is a convergence claim in disguise. A cap is a refusal boundary and never a second success condition, so reaching it returns BudgetExhausted, which is not a pass. The run floor stops a loop exiting on its first evaluation because that evaluation happened to look settled. Every tolerance is dimensionless (decision 0023) and an absolute tolerance is refused at construction, which is the rule the oracle registry applies to a threshold, applied here to a loop.

The finalizer re-evaluates every loop's exit at the final state and reports pass, fail naming the loop, or not evaluable. It verifies and does not iterate, and it never substitutes a coarser artifact for the one a predicate needs; a predicate that cannot be evaluated on what the run produced returns NotEvaluable by name, and a NotEvaluable is not a pass.

A loop left open on purpose is a declared absence whose cost is measured and reported, never an assumption read as a result (REQ-SYS-007).

title: Exchange and exchange!: the destination's operators, the closed ledger, the residual classifier
description:
Exchange names the two components, the quantities crossing and the conserved quantities that must balance: mass, energy, water, salt, carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and angular momentum for the atmosphere. exchange! coarsens or refines by the destination's declared operators, computes each ledger over the interval, and refuses if any is open.

Three rules, each from a recorded failure. One owner per flux, and a flux handed over is never recomputed by the receiver (REQ-SYS-009), because a receiver that recomputes has a second definition of the quantity. Ledgers are computed on in-memory state and never on written output, because a check that reads a file measures the file's quantum first. The tolerance is derived rather than chosen and is read from Reductions where the fields plan puts it, so a ledger tolerance has one definition.

An accelerated or replayed forcing declares which terms are replayed and which are recomputed against the live receiving state; terms that depend on the receiver's prognostic state are always recomputed.

title: 89 born-digital papers carry a broken font encoding; their equations and constants extract corrupt
description:
Found on 2026-09-10 while checking a page citation. Dessert 2003 page 6 prints fw = Rf x 18.41 exp(0.0553 T) and extracts as:

  fw ¼ Rf  18:41 expd0:0553 T P

Substitutions are systematic: equals becomes the vulgar fraction one quarter, the decimal point inside a number becomes a colon, parentheses become eth and thorn, the multiplication sign is dropped, and the degree sign becomes a lowercase j, so 16 degrees C reads as '16 jC'.

NOT an extractor bug and not fixable by swapping one. pdftotext, pypdf and pdfium all produce the same characters, and installing fontTools, which pypdf's own warning suggests, changes nothing. The publisher shipped subsetted Type1 fonts declaring WinAnsiEncoding with a glyph mapping that does not match and no ToUnicode table, so the codepoints in the file genuinely are those characters. Anything reading the text layer will reproduce it.

Scale: 89 of 736 papers, all 89 read by pdftotext in reading-order mode, none of the 230 read by Chandra. About 7143 lines carry at least one of the substitutions.

The damage is narrow and badly placed. Body prose is clean, so semantic retrieval still works and did find this paper. What is corrupt is the display-math font: equations, coefficients, exponents and unit symbols. That is exactly what a constant with the Sourced disposition is transcribed from. A person reading the extracted page copies 18:41 and jC; rg for a printed coefficient returns nothing, which defeats what extract_text.py exists to provide.

Fix: read them with the OCR chain rather than the text layer. Chandra reads pixels, returns equations as LaTeX, and already produced clean output for the other 230. These are born-digital so they were never routed there. Add the 89 to a pass and record in extract_text.py why these files are exempt from the text-layer route, or the next run will quietly overwrite the OCR with pdftotext again.
acceptance_criteria: rg for a coefficient printed in any of the 89 papers finds it at the right page, and a positive control shows the repair leaves already-clean papers unchanged.

Gates on how the vulgar fraction is used, not how often, and emits a per-page repair list in the format chandra_pages.py --repair already takes. 841 pages in 88 papers, of 28997 read, so the repair is 841 pages rather than the 2096 a whole-paper re-read would cost. Controls: Dessert 2003 page 6 listed with 18 damage marks, page 7 not listed with none; the IEEE floating-point standard excluded, its plus-or-minus one quarter being a real fraction.

title: The index name changes when ask.py is imported instead of run, so an importer sees an empty index
description:
PaperQA derives the index directory name from a hash whose segments include get_stable_str(settings.parsing.parse_pdf), and for a function that string is '<module>.<qualname>'. ask.py assigns its own parser, so the name is '__main__.parse_from_extracted_text' when ask.py runs as a script and 'ask.parse_from_extracted_text' when anything imports it.

The 377 MB index built by ask.py --build lives at pqa_index_cf50d05045ca4aed8ea18ce5e1321e61 and is reachable only from the script path. An importer computes pqa_index_cae4ac318a4d215ec55cc8c5f46b44bc, finds nothing, and either raises 'Index ... was empty, please rebuild it' or, on a build, silently starts a second copy of the archive. I created that empty directory while instrumenting and removed it again.

tools/references/calib/retrieve_index.py imports ask, so it is on the wrong side of this. It happens to open the index by explicit name rather than through get_directory_index, which is why it has not been bitten.

Fix by pinning the index name rather than letting it be derived: AgentSettings.index takes a name, and paperqa.toml is where it belongs, so the index a build wrote is the index a query opens however either was invoked.

title: PaperQA2 citations come back as 'Unknown authors', overwriting the manifest citation
description: ask.py writes references/index/manifest.csv with a verbatim 'title. identifier. [file.pdf]' citation per source, and sets use_doc_details=False so no network metadata lookup happens. PaperQA's process_file passes each manifest row through DocDetails(**row).model_dump() before Docs.aadd sees it. DocDetails.populate_bibtex_key_citation regenerates the bibtex whenever a row carries none (a manifest row never does), and because 'citation', 'key' and 'docname' are in DEFAULT_FIELDS_TO_OVERWRITE_FROM_METADATA it then discards the manifest citation and reformats it from that bibtex. Every indexed source therefore carries 'Unknown authors. <lowercased title>. Unknown journal, Unknown year.' and a docname like 'unknownauthorsUnknownyear...'. Both are stored in the index, so the 736 already-indexed sources keep the wrong strings until they are rewritten.
design: Name the fields ask.py sets itself in a fields_to_overwrite_from_metadata manifest column, so PaperQA keeps the citation and docname the manifest carries. Add a repair that rewrites those two fields in the stored Docs in place, since re-embedding the archive to correct a string is not warranted.
acceptance_criteria: A fresh manifest row round-trips through DocDetails with its citation unchanged; every indexed source in references/index reports the manifest citation and the PDF stem as its docname.
close_reason: Manifest now names fields_to_overwrite_from_metadata, so PaperQA keeps the row's citation and docname; --relabel rewrote the 736 already-indexed records in place. Verified: manifest round-trip through DocDetails is byte-identical, no record in references/index still says Unknown authors, embeddings and chunk counts unchanged, --build reports nothing to do. Commit cdfa2a6.

title: ask.py rebuilt the embedding model per document and ran on the CPU
description: The Settings.get_embedding_model override returned a new InstructedSTEmbedding on every call, and PaperQA calls it once per document in aadd_texts. The first of 736 instances loaded onto the card and took 17.6 GB; every later one saw too little free VRAM and loaded on the CPU in bfloat16. The card sat full and idle while 13 cores ran an 8B embedder. Evidence: notes/findings/2026-09-09-embedding-model-reloaded-per-document.md.
acceptance_criteria: The model is one instance for the life of the process, verified by identity across repeated get_embedding_model calls and across separate settings() calls. The chosen device is printed once with the free VRAM that decided it. A rebuild shows a non-empty SM column for the build process in nvidia-smi pmon.
notes:
Verified 2026-09-10, two of the three criteria.

ONE INSTANCE: seven get_embedding_model calls across two separate settings() objects, plus embedding_from_config() directly, return one object by identity. The per-document rebuild is gone. The construction now has one door, embedding_from_config(), which both ask.py's Settings subclass and calib/retrieve_index.py come through, so there is no second place to reintroduce it.

ONE ANNOUNCEMENT: the device line printed once, not once per document: 'embedding model on cpu (2.5 GiB free on the card, threshold 18; embedding_device=auto)'.

NOT YET VERIFIED: the nvidia-smi pmon criterion, which wants a non-empty SM column for the build process. It needs the card, and the card is serving Chandra for the OCR repair pass with 2.5 GiB free, so the embedder correctly chose the CPU and there is nothing for pmon to show. Run it when the card is free: ask.py --reingest on one paper is enough to put a document through the embedder without rebuilding the archive.
close_reason:
All three criteria met, the third with a caveat about how it can be measured.

ONE INSTANCE: seven get_embedding_model calls across two separate settings() objects, plus embedding_from_config(), return one object by identity. Construction has one door that ask.py and calib/retrieve_index.py both use.

ONE ANNOUNCEMENT, WITH THE FREE VRAM THAT DECIDED IT: 'embedding model on cuda (19.6 GiB free on the card, threshold 18; embedding_device=auto)', printed once for the whole build rather than once per document.

ON THE CARD: during ask.py --build the process held 16.8 to 17.4 GB of device memory and the card ran at 86 to 98 percent SM, sampled twelve times.

CAVEAT for whoever writes the next GPU criterion: the SM column against the build process itself is empty, and that does not mean the card is idle. qrun enforces its vram cap through MPS, so a job is an MPS client, nvidia-smi pmon types it M+C and reports its SM as '-', and the utilisation appears against the nvidia-cuda-mps-server process instead. Read SM from the MPS server row and device memory from the client row, or from --query-compute-apps. A criterion that reads only the client's SM column will report a working card as idle.

title: Triage the 1750 OCR'd table pages for digital-native replacements before any re-read
description: 1750 pages carrying a table were read by OCR at the old pixel cap; the 19042 pages from digital-native sources are not affected. Before re-reading anything, each source is asked whether a digital-native source exists for what its tables carry, the way NIST-JANAF was replaced by the NASA CEA polynomials. Three groups came out of the first cut: 719 table pages in 22 paywalled works that certainly exist born-digital, now listed in docs/references/REQUESTS.md; 150 in 7 openly published reports where a publisher copy exists but may itself be OCR, so each needs a quality comparison rather than an assumption; and the remainder with no substitute.
acceptance_criteria: Every source with OCR'd table pages carries a disposition: replaced by a machine-readable dataset, replaced by a born-digital copy, or re-read at the raised cap. No source is re-read before its disposition is decided, and no source is left with OCR'd tables and no disposition.
notes:
Carmichael's Handbook of Physical Properties of Rocks is the largest single item at 239 table pages and is held only for rock spectra from Hunt's chapter. ECOSTRESS and USGS splib07 are already held as machine-readable input datasets covering that, so it is a candidate for removal outright rather than replacement. Confirm what it actually anchors before deleting.

The two USGS reports fetched as a test both carry a real text layer, but pass 2 of the reading chain existed to replace publisher text layers judged worse than Chandra, so a text layer is not by itself a reason to swap back.
close_reason: Resolved by a different route than the row assumed. OCR'd table cells are removed from the queryable text corpus-wide (tools/references/strip_ocr_tables.py, 1889 tables on 1511 pages, now the last step of the reading chain), so no unverifiable number is quotable with a page citation. The per-book triage was the wrong shape: most scanned sources are held for a scheme, not for numbers. The dataset question is asked per constant as constants are filed; JANAF to CEA and Carmichael to ECOSTRESS/splib07 are done. The born-digital book requests are withdrawn.

title: Decide what happens to the 255 tables the reader invented from figures
description: 255 tables on 224 pages across 57 sources are numbers read off a plot by the OCR, not transcribed from a page: 3839 rows in all. Every one captions itself as estimated from a figure, which is a reliable handle. Confirmed against the scan by eye on Brutsaert page 182 and Sakai page 50. Evidence: notes/findings/2026-09-09-tables-invented-from-figures.md. The detector is in tools/references/audit_tables_by_shape.py. Raising the pixel cap does not touch this; it is what ocr_layout was asked to do.
acceptance_criteria: No page of references/text presents figure-derived numbers in the same markup as transcribed ones. Whichever way it is settled, deletion or fencing, the count of remaining invented tables reported by tools/references/audit_tables_by_shape.py over the whole corpus is zero, and a page that had one still reads correctly as prose.
notes: This is a decision, not a cleanup: deleting loses a digitisation someone might have wanted, and fencing keeps content the sources do not contain. Raise it as a decision record rather than settling it in a commit. Whatever is chosen also applies to future reads, so it belongs with the prompt the reader is given, not only with the text already produced.
close_reason: Done: the 255 invented tables are stripped with tools/references/strip_invented_tables.py, leaving a marker naming the figure; Henderson's duplicated column is removed and its four cancelled rows marked from the strikethrough on the scan.

title: Read the NASA CEA polynomials, and cross-check them against Burcat and Ruscic
description: Thermochemical data enters the model from docs/inputs/data/nasa-cea-thermo.toml, not from OCR. Needed: a reader for the fixed-width 9-term records that selects the temperature interval and refuses a temperature outside the record's range rather than extrapolating, evaluation of Cp, H and S, and formation quantities. Every constant taken from here cites the record and the volume its reference-date code names, not the file. The Burcat/Ruscic set at docs/inputs/data/burcat-ruscic-thermochemical.toml is the second source, read only for a species CEA lacks or an Active Thermochemical Tables enthalpy that beats CEA's, and either case is an exception named on the constant.
acceptance_criteria: A species evaluated from the coefficients reproduces the printed NIST-JANAF fourth edition table for that species to the tolerance of the fit, read from the scan by eye at a handful of temperatures spanning the record's range. The two identities in tools/references/audit_janaf_tables.py hold for the evaluated values. The reader refuses, rather than mis-parses, the roughly 100 records whose long names push the later fields out of their nominal columns.
notes:
CEA carries TiO, VO, Ti, V, Fe, Mg, Na, K and AL2O3 with its phases, which Burcat lacked, and 255 records reach 20000 K. Names are upper case for metals and carry a phase suffix for condensed polymorphs; a reader must not assume the mixed case of the gas-phase organics.

2026-09-10: the JANAF half of this row is gone. The scanned fourth edition has been removed from the archive outright, so there is no by-eye check against a printed table for the 214 j-coded records. The cross-check is against Burcat and Ruscic where the species overlaps, which is machine-readable on both sides and a better check than a page read by eye. Nothing here is blocked; the earlier note claiming an OCR blocker is superseded.
close_reason: Not carried: the source switched from the scanned NIST-JANAF fourth edition to machine-readable NASA CEA and Burcat/Ruscic, and the scan has been removed from the archive, so the by-eye cross-read this row was built around has no value. The reader half (CEA fixed-width records, interval selection, refusal outside range, Burcat/Ruscic as second source) is carried on the M3 plan row fiddlybits-84a.1, which owns the gas-mixture property group of REQ-ATM-017.

title: Re-read the 421 JANAF pages whose tables break their own identities
description: The finished Chandra read of the NIST-JANAF fourth edition is clean in prose and damaged in the tables: 421 of 1095 data pages break one of the two arithmetic identities the printed columns must satisfy, or lost a cell outright. Failure modes are a column slid by one row, a column duplicated over its neighbour, and a column dropped with the header cells merged. None of them is visible in the output. Evidence and the shapes of the damage: notes/findings/2026-09-09-janaf-table-identities.md. The page list is references/work/janaf_repair_list.txt, in the form chandra_pages.py --repair takes.
acceptance_criteria: tools/references/audit_janaf_tables.py --self-test passes, and a re-read of the listed pages leaves no page reported by tools/references/audit_janaf_tables.py over references/text/chase1998-nist-janaf-thermochemical-tables-fourth-edition. Pages that still fail after a second read are listed with their kind rather than silently accepted.
notes:
The audit constrains four of the eight columns. The heat capacity, the entropy and the enthalpy of formation have nothing testing them, so a clean audit is a floor and not a warrant; a page carrying a constant into the model is still checked against the scan by eye.

These pages were already read upright: the manifest records pages_turned_upright=1335 at long_side_px=3300 for this file, so orientation is not the cause and repeating the read at the same settings is not a fix but a coin flip. The lever to try first is the render resolution and the tiling the server is given, since the defect is a dense eight-column table transcribed at a pixel budget that blurs column boundaries. Measure a handful of the twelve wholly corrupt pages at a higher long side before committing the card to all 421.
close_reason: Superseded: the JANAF scan is no longer a data path. The same numbers are machine-readable as NASA polynomial fits in the Burcat/Ruscic database, fetched and manifested at docs/inputs/data/burcat-ruscic-thermochemical.toml, so re-reading 493 scanned pages buys nothing. The scan stays as a check, not a source.

title: Settle the reporting-limiter question when the free-boundary solvers are built
description:
An open consideration recorded in decisions 0019, 0020 and 0035, to be settled at implementation and never before.

REQ-HYD-004 and REQ-CRY-001 forbid a clip at the water table and the ice margin, because a clip invents water or ice and the ledgers those components close at every step would refuse it. The reference-tree survey found that the mature adjacent codebases clip anyway, which they can afford because they close no such ledger, so this project is on an unpaved road.

The middle position, not currently admitted by the records: a limiter that writes its invented or destroyed mass to the ledger and refuses above a registered tolerance is a different thing from a silent clamp. The question is whether that reporting form is admissible in the fast profile while the free-boundary solver is being earned, or whether the absolute prohibition stands.

Settle it against evidence, not preference: the measured ledger residual of a reporting limiter at two mesh levels, the residual's time signature (leak against roundoff), and whether any result quoted from the fast profile would be changed by it. If admitted, it is a bounded fallback with the residual reported beside every result that used it, never a licence to clip.
acceptance_criteria: A decision recorded in 0019 and 0020 with the measurement that settled it; the risk-register row updated; if admitted, the reporting requirement and the registered tolerance stated.
notes: Milestone label m2 is an inference, not a reading: this row's description names no milestone, unlike the other 22 under the epic. REQ-HYD-004's water table is a free boundary built at M2 (decision 0019) and REQ-CRY-001's ice margin at M10 (decision 0020), so M2 is the first point at which the question must be answered. Move it if the water-table solver slips.

title: Settle whether pseudo-transient relaxation can carry an active-set outer loop
description: M2. docs/surveys/terrain-ice-and-solvers.md, revisited at M10. The water table and the ice margin are both obstacle problems. The mature reference codebases clip instead: a shallow-ice solver clips thickness with a plain conditional and a bound-constrained sample solver does the same, which is what this project's requirements reject, so nobody adjacent has paved this road. Establish whether the pseudo-transient iteration admits a projection step or whether a different iteration is needed.
notes: Labelled milestone:m2, the milestone it is wanted by. The description's 'revisited at M10' still holds: the ice-margin obstacle problem re-opens the same question in the cryosphere block.

title: Choose the complementarity oracle arm: the open GPU solver against the licensed one
description: M2. docs/surveys/terrain-ice-and-solvers.md and docs/surveys/sciml.md, a cross-group finding neither surveyor could see alone. Decision 0019 formulates the water table as a box-constrained complementarity problem and decision 0025 wants an independent arm. One candidate is licence-encumbered with a bounded free tier that covers identity-scale checks but perhaps not the mutation run; the other is open with native GPU-batched projected relaxation. Decide which is the arm and which, if either, informs the in-house solver.

title: Read the flow-routing kernels: take the tree contraction, leave the raster
description: M2. docs/surveys/terrain-ice-and-solvers.md. The accumulation is an exact rake-and-compress form of the linear-time tree sum, and the basin merge is an exact parallel minimum-spanning construction, but the depression routing fills to the spill unconditionally with no water volume in the construction, which decision 0019 rejects. The neighbour and basin-adjacency kernels are hardcoded to four raster offsets and do not survive on a triangle mesh; the pointer-jumping tree contraction touches no coordinates and would carry over to the connectivity graph unchanged.

title: Carve out the closed-form Kepler solve
description: M0. docs/surveys/orbits-and-stellar.md. A closed-form non-iterative scalar solve valid across the whole elliptic range sits in two files of a package whose remainder is keyed to Julian dates and is dismissed with the ephemeris cluster. Read it as an algorithm for decision 0008's requirement, not as a dependency, and pair it with the bracketing solver row above.
close_reason: read: docs/imports/astrolib-jl.md. Markley's closed form is carried with the half of the paper AstroLib omits: equations 30 to 35, the residual and derivative that hold near unit eccentricity. As implemented it reaches 5.35e-07 relative in the region the paper names; with the fix, under one ulp of pi everywhere. Paper fetched (green OA), read and indexed.

title: Read the carbonate-chemistry solvers against the composition fence
description: M6. docs/surveys/biogeochemistry-and-conceptual.md. Two independent implementations compute boron, sulfate and fluoride as literal ratios to salinity, which decision 0017 now requires derived from the declared composition. The question for the closer look is whether their equilibrium-constant machinery is separable from those defaults, or whether the ratios are structural.

title: Read the conceptual-model and change-point instruments for the loop's exits
description: M0. docs/surveys/biogeochemistry-and-conceptual.md. Decision 0023 requires every exit evaluable and forbids declaring convergence on a system merely wandering slowly. Low-order energy balance and box models give closed-form or well-characterised bifurcation structure for a first-tier oracle, and a change-point package working on an observed series is a closer match to a drift criterion than attractor machinery, because a drift criterion sees a series and not a system with a known rule.
close_reason: read: docs/imports/exit-criteria-instruments.md. None of the three can be a dependency (ConceptualClimateModels reaches FastPower transitively, which the manifest check refuses). What carries is the surrogate null from TransitionsInTimeseries, reimplemented: a phase-randomised surrogate of the run's own series replaces REQ-NUM-001's autocorrelation-corrected standard error and makes no stationarity assumption. Two registry entries added, including the positive control decision 0023's exit criteria lacked: a trajectory crawling along a slow manifold that the criteria must refuse to call converged.

title: Settle the fast-tier integrator: the candidate against the alternative
description: M0. docs/surveys/sciml.md and docs/imports/climatimesteppers-jl.md. The schemes overlap, but one arrives welded to a stack decision 0012 declined. This is the sub-decision decision 0012 says it does not take: the transitive dependency and how the device is built from the profile, a convergence checker so a non-converged stage cannot pass silently, and the tableau choice.
close_reason: settled as a proposed decision: docs/decisions/0041-fast-tier-integrator.md. ClimaTimeSteppers under five conditions (device from the profile, a refusing convergence checker, SSP333 under the SSP constraint because the fast tier carries a limiter, the tableau element type set explicitly, and OrdinaryDiffEq excluded by the FastPower manifest check). Two oracle entries added; Gardner 2018 fetched and held, Ascher 1997 requested. The record is proposed and awaits the user.

title: Import review: the bracketing root solvers, and a portable-kernel launch test
description: M0. docs/surveys/sciml.md. Non-allocating scalar iteration with a tolerance derived from the type, demonstrated solving from inside a device kernel in the tree's own tests. Decision 0008 needs Kepler to rounding for any eccentricity below one; the column physics needs the same in several places. The gap is that the demonstration uses the vendor kernel macro rather than the portable one this project adopted, so the record must include that test.

The portable-kernel launch test was written and run: ITP and Bisection through SciMLBase.solve run under the KernelAbstractions CPU backend and fail to compile for CUDA, because each solver's not-an-enclosing-interval branch carries a SciMLLogging call. title: Read DimensionalData's broadcast machinery before Field is written
description: M0. docs/surveys/gpu-and-arrays.md. How it threads compile-time metadata through Julia's broadcast pipeline without allocating or dropping type parameters, which decision 0006 needs for Field. Its adaptation extension also strips string-bearing metadata at the device boundary deliberately, a worked precedent for the same boundary provenance will hit.

title: Import review: AcceleratedKernels.jl, with the thread-count invariance fix as a gate
description: M0. docs/surveys/gpu-and-arrays.md. Its default processor-side reduction chunks by the thread count, so its default sum is not thread-count invariant, which decision 0029 makes a design property tested by repeats. The record must carry pinning the chunking at every call site as a checklist item, and the leak test that would catch a bare call.

title: Import review: StructArrays.jl, StaticArrays.jl for the cells-first layout
description: M0. docs/surveys/gpu-and-arrays.md. Struct-of-arrays storage with array-of-structs syntax, with adaptation and backend extensions already present and tested, which is what decision 0011's cells-first layout wants for a column state struct. Produce records in docs/imports/ against the checklist, and the decision an adoption would need.

title: Read CombinatorialSpaces DEC operators, and settle the chordal-subdivision gap
description: M0. docs/surveys/mesh-and-discretisation.md. Its circumcentric duals, both Hodge star forms, sharp and flat operators and portable wedge kernels are close to what decision 0013's triangle C-grid needs, on a sphere, with connectivity as explicit tables. But BinarySubdivision.propagate_points places a new vertex at the flat chordal midpoint of its parents with no renormalisation onto the sphere, which is not the great-circle bisection decision 0005's exact-nesting argument rests on. Settle what that costs and whether their operator definitions survive the correction, before the mesh module is written.
close_reason: settled: the flat midpoint freezes the surface at the base level's polyhedron and the correction is one exact normalisation; the DEC operators survive it unchanged because they are Euclidean throughout, which is the reason they are a reference and not a dependency. docs/imports/combinatorialspaces-jl.md, notes/findings/2026-09-10-chordal-bisection-and-spherical-area.md, two registry thresholds sharpened

description:
About 870 repositories were cloned to /home/cfutro/git for reading: sixteen organisation folders and nineteen standalone packages, listed in /home/cfutro/reference_repos.md with the reasoning in /home/cfutro/reference_repos_desc.md. The CliMA folder is already surveyed and is skipped here.

title: Import review: RootSolvers.jl, and what Kepler to rounding needs
description: The sweep flagged RootSolvers.jl as sitting on the adoptable side of decision 0012's line: Brent, bisection, regula falsi, secant and Newton with and without automatic differentiation, broadcastable inside a kernel, tolerances supplied by the caller as types rather than chosen numbers, and only ForwardDiff and Printf as dependencies. Decision 0008 now requires Kepler's equation solved to rounding for any eccentricity below one, which is exactly this. Write docs/imports/rootsolvers-jl.md: what of it would be used, whether the broadcast path is allocation free on the device, what its ForwardDiff dependency implies for decision 0033 (differentiability deferred), and the verdict with the leak test.
acceptance_criteria: docs/imports/rootsolvers-jl.md complete; the in-kernel and allocation questions answered from source; the ForwardDiff implication for 0033 stated.
notes: Read at 7389b926dd93bad4d872f4b50a1e49208167fa3f (2026-09-01). In-kernel and allocation questions answered: the bracketed loop is branch-free ifelse arithmetic with no exception, no I/O and no allocation, and the tree asserts isbits results and zero allocations in test/test_fval_inputs.jl and test/runtests.jl:158; NoTolerance plus TwoPointSolution is a documented fixed-cost data-independent device solve. The gap is that the GPU demonstration is broadcast over a CuArray, vendor-specific, with no KernelAbstractions dependency and no portable-kernel test, which is the same gap fiddlybits-bon.6 names. ForwardDiff implication for 0033: two call sites only (base_type at line 84, value_deriv at 1947) and only NewtonsMethodAD reaches them, so the dependency is severable, but it is a hard dep rather than an extension; and the tree's own comment records sin(::Dual) failing GPU codegen, which is evidence for 0033's tool-maturity bullet. Verdict adopt-subject-to-a-wrapper. Corrects the organisation sweep on one point: tolerances are typed and caller-supplied, but find_zero still applies a chosen default of 1e-4 (Float64) or 1e-3 when none is passed, which is twelve orders short of the rounding decision 0008 requires and is silent.
close_reason: completed: docs/imports/rootsolvers-jl.md written against the checklist; in-kernel and allocation questions answered from source; ForwardDiff implication for decision 0033 stated

title: Import review: CGDycore.jl, the one CliMA grid machinery that is not cubed-sphere only
description: The organisation sweep flagged CGDycore.jl as the strongest find: src/Grids/Triangular.jl builds node, edge and face lists and refines by projecting edge midpoints onto the unit sphere, which is icosahedral refinement, beside hexagonal, kite, Healpix and equal-area grids, with explicit connectivity modules, on KernelAbstractions across CUDA and Metal. That is the one repository in CliMA whose grid machinery is not welded to the cubed sphere, and it bears directly on decisions 0005 (the mesh) and 0006 (Field). Read the source and write docs/imports/cgdycore-jl.md to the survey's format: what the triangular grid actually constructs, whether the refinement nests exactly the way decision 0005 requires, whether connectivity is a derived graph or an emergent property, what the data layout assumes, and the verdict with the leak test any adopt recommendation would need.
acceptance_criteria: docs/imports/cgdycore-jl.md complete against the checklist, read at a pinned commit, with the nesting question answered from source.
notes: Read at 9dfd007f2c600576dd276e53c00fb817dffca7a8 (2026-08-18). Nesting question answered from source and favourably: MidPoint in src/Grids/Triangular.jl normalises the chordal midpoint onto the sphere, which is exact great-circle bisection, unlike the CombinatorialSpaces gap in fiddlybits-bon.1. Sibling ordering also lands on children(i)=4i-3:4i as a side effect of the in-place list surgery, but the hierarchy is numbered once at the end and discarded, and refinement is global only with no 2:1 balance. Verdict borrow-ideas-only: storage is array-of-structs with per-cell heap vectors, the radius is baked into the mesh, and there is no test suite anywhere in the tree, so nothing is demonstrated. Two findings worth carrying: PhysParameters accepts ScaleFactor and does not apply it to the radius the flag is named for, leaving two live radii on any reduced-radius run; ConnectivityGraph stores multiplicities rather than the 1s the code appears to write, because sparse() sums duplicate index pairs.
close_reason: completed: docs/imports/cgdycore-jl.md written against the docs/imports/README.md checklist item by item, read at a pinned commit, nesting question answered from source

title: Survey the CliMA ecosystem for what this project can adopt, borrow or must reject
description:

title: System{FT}: stars, planet, moons, inventories, numerics; keyword-only, no defaults; Derived fields computed and checked against a supplied value; strip() to isbits constants
description:

Star declares mass, age and metallicity as primaries with luminosity, effective temperature, radius and spectrum Derived from a carried stellar model or Bracketed, the radius never absent. Everything a profile may vary is Profile's (52v.4.8) and the suite asserts the two structs' field names are disjoint.

Orbit sits above Systems in the include order, so Orbit.check_eccentricity, which 52v.10 merged, cannot be what the constructor calls; 52v.5.3 removes it. The equinox kind's refusals (obliquity below the rounding threshold, no single primary) fire here too.

description:
Ledger{Q} carrying the balance of one conserved quantity across one operation with an inventory of what was lost and to where. Every operator returns (field, ledger) and the store refuses a field whose ledger is open.

The tolerance is k*N*eps*M read from Reductions rather than declared here, so a ledger tolerance has one definition (REQ-NUM-004, REQ-SYS-103). A tolerance chosen per ledger is what let the predecessor's nitrogen closure be judged against a bar larger than the quantum of the column it differenced.

A residual's time signature is classified rather than reported as a number: linear growth is a leak, a constant offset is a stock omitted from the inventory, a random walk of rounding size is rounding. The three have different fixes and the report names the class.

title: Connectivity graph derived from a terrain-level field: strait sill depth and width between coarse ocean cells, land contiguity, basin terminals; topology-change events
description:
The connectivity graph derived from a terrain-level field every slow step: for each pair of adjacent coarse ocean cells the minimum sill depth and the width of their connection; for land, contiguity; for basins, the drainage terminal.

A surface class is decided by connectivity to the world ocean and never by the sign of elevation (REQ-TER-012). Land, ocean and inland-water fractions are exact areas from the terrain level, and a cell with a fraction strictly between zero and one holds an island or lake tile: an island is never rounded to ocean and a strait is never rounded to land.

A topology change is an event, not a diagnostic. A seaway closing, a land bridge flooding or a basin capturing its neighbour forces a climate refresh, so a closure happens when it happens rather than being averaged away by the slow tier. The kind comes from the closed vocabulary of decision 0042 and is emitted through the one emitter, never written here.

The physics of strait exchange, the discharge coefficients and the overflow closure are decision 0031's second layer and belong to the ocean milestone. This row builds the graph those read, and its geometry.

title: Local refinement: variable-level meshes with 2:1 balance, hanging-edge flux bookkeeping, graded transition rings of declared width for fluid components, and the refinement region API
description:
Variable-level meshes 2:1 balanced by construction rather than by repair, with hanging edges carrying their own flux-conserving measure so a flux through a coarse edge equals the sum over its children exactly. That exactness is what lets the ledgers of decision 0009 demand identity rather than tolerance.

Fluid refinement is graded and damped refinement may be abrupt: atmosphere and ocean step down one level at a time through transition rings of a declared minimum width in cells with divergence damping inside the transition, because an abrupt 2:1 step reflects gravity and acoustic waves and seeds grid-scale storms at the boundary; terrain, hydrology and the land column use abrupt boundaries. The ring width is read from the profile, never a constant here.

The refinement region API takes a region and a depth in levels. Invoking refinement from a sensitivity instrument is decision 0031's third layer and belongs to the feature records that declare the metrics; this row provides the mechanism a probe calls, not the probe.

description:
Both dual measures at every level and inside every refinement region, each named and never an unqualified area: primal cell area, dual cell area, primal edge length, dual edge length, the circumcentre as the named dual vertex, and the primal-to-dual edge angle as a tested property (REQ-TER-011). No function accepts an area without saying which.

Cell area takes the Van Oosterom and Strackee vector form, with l'Huilier kept as the second arm of the identity. The two agree with a 400-bit reference at that precision and disagree at working precision by a known factor: about an eighth of an epsilon of absolute error per cell against about one epsilon. Two arms that agree at high precision are what let the identity tell a formula defect from rounding.

A per-cell identity is bounded in absolute area and never in relative area, since a relative bar would loosen by four per level to stay true; a sum over cells is bounded by the cell count times that absolute floor. Both thresholds are already in the registry in that form.

Mesh geometry is built and stored in double precision whatever the component's working type: at level 7 the vector form in FP32 is already wrong in the fourth digit. Support carries the type its geometry was formed in.

The radius reaches both measures through exactly one function, applied at the point of use and never multiplied into stored coordinates.

title: Base icosahedron and bisection with hierarchical numbering: children(i)=4i-3:4i, parent(i)=(i+3)>>2, 1-based in memory, 0-based on disk via CellId
description:
The base icosahedron constructed from the golden ratio in the working type, and bisection that renormalises at every level. The shipped icosphere artifact of CombinatorialSpaces.jl is not a source of vertex positions: it is a Blender export at six decimal places, nine orders above the rounding these identities are measured at (notes/findings/2026-09-10-chordal-bisection-and-spherical-area.md).

Renormalisation is not a refinement of the midpoint but the midpoint itself: for two unit vectors the chord midpoint lies in the plane through them and the origin and bisects their angle, so normalising it gives the great-circle midpoint exactly. Without it every new vertex stays in the plane of its parent triangle, the surface never leaves the base polyhedron, and refinement buys resolution with no convergence.

children(i) = 4i-3:4i and parent(i) = (i+3)>>2, 1-based in memory and 0-based on disk, with CellId crossing that boundary refusing arithmetic so a mixed-base defect is a type error. children returning a contiguous range is what makes a coarsening a segmented reduction over a power-of-four segment.

title: Nothing obliges a certification to run the exhaustive degree-five arm beside the sampled one
description:
fiddlybits-52v.7.17 built Backends.exhaustive_envelope and the sites door, and put them BESIDE the sampled envelope rather than inside it, which is what notes/findings/2026-09-11-ulp-ensemble-member-count.md asked for so the declared miss rate keeps its meaning. That part is right and should not be undone.

What is missing is the obligation. certify(kernel, case, env) takes whatever envelope its caller built. A caller who builds only the sampled envelope gets exactly the blind spot fiddlybits-52v.7.17 exists to close, and gets it silently, with a PASS. Today the only thing that runs both arms is test/certify/degree_five.jl. A future certification of a real kernel will not.

Settle how the obligation is carried. Options, not a decision: a single entry point that takes a case and returns both verdicts, so a caller cannot ask for one; a refusal when a case built on a mesh support is certified against an envelope whose sites do not cover the degree-five vertices; or a registry-level rule that a certification result is not admissible without both arms named. The last is the cheapest and the weakest.

Whatever is chosen, a caller must not be able to reach a PASS that skipped the twelve sites without saying so.

title: Settle the lint_literals exemption for the transcendental coefficient tables
description:
fiddlybits-52v.7.8 added Backends/transcendentals.jl to lint_literals' exempt list so the gate would pass, and argued it in a comment in test/lint/lists/literals.toml. The argument is sound as far as it goes: a Taylor or minimax coefficient table and an argument-reduction split are bit patterns of the precision they belong to, not values a caller supplies a type for, so T(0.1666...) would be wrong rather than merely awkward, since a Float32 set is a different fit and not a rounded Float64 one.

Two things are wrong with how it stands.

The exemption is per file and blanket, so anything later added to that file escapes REQ-NUM-001 entirely, including a genuine precision defect that has nothing to do with a coefficient table. A narrower mechanism would exempt the tables rather than the file: literals inside a const whose name matches the declared table pattern, or an explicit per-constant allowance in the list.

And the argument lives in a comment. Decision 0039 puts an argument in docs/decisions/ and lets a comment name it by path. Widening the scope of a lint that enforces a requirement is a decision about that requirement's reach, not a configuration detail, and it was taken inside a row about polynomials.

The solve needs a Backend to switch on. Orbit sits above Backends in the include order, so it may read it. Whether the Backend reaches eccentric_anomaly as an argument or as a type parameter is the row's judgement.

title: Decide whether bitwise-mode multiply-add kernels should route through muladd instead of the @noinline barrier
description: notes/findings/2026-09-11-gpucompiler-unconditional-fma-contraction.md measured that Backends.nofuse_mul's @noinline barrier makes the CPU and GPU backends agree by moving the GPU to the CPU's two-rounding answer (both one ulp off the reference at the tested magnitude), while Julia's muladd is bitwise identical across backends and correctly rounded on both, because the CPU backend on the measured host also lowers muladd to a hardware fused multiply-add. This row decides whether decision 0029's bitwise mode should prefer muladd where a kernel's source shape allows a bare multiply feeding a bare add, keep the barrier where it does not (Backends.stencil_gather_bitwise_kernel! accumulates into a running sum, not a bare add), or some mix, and whether the choice can rely on hardware FMA being present on every backend the project certifies bitwise mode on. A design judgement with a numerical argument inside it: tier:frontier.
notes: Decided and applied: bitwise mode writes every multiply that feeds an add as an explicit fma; the @noinline barrier keeps only the role its name describes, a product that must be rounded on its own. docs/decisions/0044-explicit-fma-in-bitwise-mode.md, amends 0029 on the mechanism. Measurements in notes/findings/2026-09-11-fma-against-the-fusion-barrier-in-bitwise-mode.md. SHAPE: acc += a*b is acc = fma(a, b, acc), so Backends.stencil_gather_bitwise_kernel! has the fused shape after all; written that way it is bitwise across the backends at every cell of the module's fixture at Float64 and Float32 and reproduces the 256-bit once-per-term chain exactly, so no kernel stays on the barrier and bitwise mode has one mechanism. title: Geometry recomputes each edge midpoint three times; ring_distance allocates a queue per ring; kahan_add! is not inlined
description:
Raised in review. Three separate things, all inside the mesh module.

geometry evaluates great_circle_midpoint, which is a square root and a division, three times for every edge: twice in the cell loop, once from each of the two cells sharing the edge, and once more in the edge loop. Splitting geometry into three passes, edge measures first, then cell and dual areas reading the midpoints back, then dual edge lengths and normals, evaluates each midpoint once. The third pass also loops over edges directly, which drops the recorded BitVector and the branch that skips an edge already seen. Floating-point addition commutes, so a midpoint read back is bitwise what the cell loop computed, and no result moves.

ring_distance allocates a fresh next vector for every ring of the breadth-first search. The queue is bounded by the cell count, so one flat vector with a head and a tail index makes the search allocation-free.

kahan_add! mutates two vectors three times per cell in the hottest loop in the module and carries bounds checks and no inlining hint.

A fourth item was raised and is not carried here: fix_winding! taking its vertices as views rather than SVectors. It runs only on the twenty cells of the base icosahedron, once per hierarchy call.

Merged at 02908e9. Suite 627 of 627. One of the four items raised survived measurement; the other three were refuted on this machine, Julia 1.12.7, best of three to ten runs with a collection between each.

Carried. The breadth-first search now walks one flat queue: searching from one seed over level 7 went from 3.462 ms and 10200 KiB to 2.089 ms and 5120 KiB.

Refuted, edge-indexed bisection. The proposal numbers a new vertex by the parent level's global edge index, which needs that level's Stencils. It does not remove the dictionary, it relocates it: stencils builds the edge numbering through a Dict of its own in build_edges, and it also builds the vertex-neighbour tables bisection has no use for. Prototyped end to end, hierarchy at level 7 went from 0.0106 s and 15.8 MiB to 0.0221 s and 29.6 MiB, so twice the time and twice the memory rather than ten times faster. It also renumbers every midpoint vertex, which changes every support digest, for no gain.

Refuted, the three-pass geometry. Each edge midpoint is evaluated three times, not seven: the cell loop evaluates three per cell, which is two per edge since there are three halves of an edge per cell, plus one in the edge loop. Removing the redundancy costs more than it saves, because a midpoint computed in registers is cheaper than a gather from a 3 by nedges matrix that is 23 MiB at level 7. Level 7 geometry went from 50.65 ms to 54.69 ms. The variant that keeps midpoints in registers and only drops the recorded BitVector by iterating edges directly is also slower, 54.76 ms, because the cell-major scan reads cells and vertices nearly in order and the edge-major one does not. Both variants were verified bitwise identical to the current form before being discarded.

Refuted, the inlined Kahan add. No measurable change, 51.44 ms against 50.65 ms, inside the run-to-run spread. Julia already inlines it, and the @inbounds would trade a bounds check on an index read out of the cells table for nothing.

Not carried, fix_winding! on SVectors: it runs on the twenty cells of the base icosahedron once per hierarchy call.

title: Bisection allocates per midpoint and copies the vertex array at every level; CellId is not scalar under broadcast
description:
Raised in review of fiddlybits-52v.2.2 after it merged at d02e627. Three things in src/Mesh/hierarchy.jl.

midpoint slices the vertex matrix, and vertices[:, a] on a standard Matrix allocates a heap Vector, so bisection allocates several small arrays per edge. Compute the three components as scalars and return a tuple.

bisect preallocates nv + 3*nc vertex columns and then returns vertices[:, 1:used], which is a full copy of the level. On a closed triangulated surface every face carries three edges and every edge two faces, so the new vertex count is exactly (3*nc) >> 1 and the array can be sized right the first time, with no trailing copy.

CellId refuses arithmetic as intended, but Julia's default broadcastable for a plain struct is collect, so a CellId used as a scalar in a broadcast raises 'no method matching length(::CellId)' rather than behaving as a scalar. Base.broadcastable(c::CellId) = Ref(c) fixes that and leaves arithmetic undefined.

Subtyping CellId as Number was proposed for the broadcast half and is refused: measured on Julia 1.12.7, a Number subtype with no promotion rule turns CellId + 1 from a MethodError into a promotion ErrorException, which breaks the acceptance of fiddlybits-52v.2.2 and advertises an arithmetic the type exists to refuse.

title: Decide the general scalar solver, when a call site exists to judge it against
description:
The Kepler question is answered by this project's own solve (decision 0008, 2026-09-10). The general scalar solve is a separate question and is deliberately left open: it wants a bracketed solve on a monotone residual, which is a different shape from a closed form, and there is no call site yet to judge a candidate against.

The first real call site is the column's saturation adjustment. Until it exists, deciding would mean choosing a package on speculation.

RootSolvers.jl remains neither adopted nor rejected. Its record already states what an adoption would need: a call site supplying its own tolerance and iteration count so the 1e-4 default is never reached, a refusal on converged == false so no caller reads a root past a failed solve, and NoTolerance with a fixed iteration count on the device so every lane does the same work. Two further things a decision must weigh: ForwardDiff enters as a hard dependency for a method this project would not call, and the bracket test is written as a product of two residuals, which underflows to -0.0 for residuals of order 1e-200 and reports a genuine sign change as no bracket. That does not bite a Kepler solve, whose endpoint residuals are of order one; it can bite a saturation adjustment on a trace condensable.

BracketingNonlinearSolve is refused for the device and its interpolate-truncate-project loop is the algorithm a project-owned bracketing loop is measured against.

title: Fix the form of the water door's general-composition fallback: not linear
description:
Decision 0017 names the general form beyond the Reference-Composition anomaly tolerance as an ion-specific Gibbs or Pitzer model and records it as a declared absence with its interface in place. It does not say what the door does in the meantime, and the seawater review turned up a result that constrains the answer.

Roquet et al. (2015, JPO), now held, concludes that a linear equation of state cannot produce a realistic thermohaline circulation: the quadratic temperature term (cabbeling) and the temperature-pressure product (thermobaricity) set the static stability below the mixed layer and therefore the surface-to-interior exchange rate. Four coefficients suffice; one does not. So a linear fallback outside the tolerance would be known-wrong rather than approximate.

Settle whether the interim fallback is a declared quadratic with its coefficients carrying dispositions, and if so what the two nonlinear terms are anchored to for a composition that is not Earth's, since the published coefficients are fitted to Earth's ocean state as well as its composition.

title: Heikes and Randall 1995 Part II is held and queued for OCR
description:
A retrieval check on 2026-09-10 asked how the twisted icosahedral grid reduces the truncation error of the discrete Laplacian. The archive holds Part I, which says only that the cells 'have been moved slightly to improve the accuracy of the finite-difference operators' and that 'the construction of this alternative, the tweaked grid is described in detail in Part II' (heikes1995 page 3). The answer therefore came mostly from Peixoto 2016 and Wan 2013, which restate the result rather than state it.

That is the case the Sourced disposition exists to prevent: the grid this project's mesh hierarchy would follow is anchored to a secondary description. Part II is where the tweaking and the accuracy analysis live.

Numerical Integration of the Shallow-Water Equations on a Twisted Icosahedral Grid. Part II. A Detailed Description of the Grid and an Analysis of Numerical Accuracy
10.1175/1520-0493(1995)123<1881:NIOTSW>2.0.CO;2

OpenAlex reports oa_status closed with no repository full text, checked 2026-09-10, so this one goes to the user rather than being fetched. Filed as requested in docs/references/INDEX.md.
acceptance_criteria: Part II is held, read and indexed, and the Laplacian truncation-error question answers from it rather than from Peixoto 2016.
notes:
Fetched by the user to /home/cfutro/requests/heikes1995.pdf and registered on 2026-09-10 as references/pdf/heikes1995-shallow-water-twisted-icosahedral-grid-ii.pdf, following Part I's name. Seven pages, 1881 to 1887, June 1995, confirmed from the rendered first page: no text layer at all, pdftotext returns 7 bytes for 7 pages, so it is a pure scan.

Queued on tools/references/pending_ocr.txt, the single list of files waiting to be read. Submitted through qrun and pending: the slurm node is DOWN or DRAINED, so nothing starts until it is resumed. Not extracted and not indexed until it is read; a build before then would record an empty read.

After the read: ask.py --build picks it up on its digest, and the ERROR entry it currently carries in the index is now treated as stale rather than adopted. Then --relabel once the INDEX.md row carries the title and DOI.

Section 2 of Part II is 'Some observations about the Laplace operator and the simple spherical geodesic grid', which is what the 2026-09-10 retrieval check could not reach.
close_reason: Part II is held, OCR'd, indexed and cited. The question that exposed the gap now answers from it: heikes1995-...-grid-ii at scores of 9 on four chunks, and Peixoto 2016 and Wan 2013, which had been restating the result, no longer appear at all. The answer names the mechanism from the source, the parameter r_i^(q), the distance between a cell wall's midpoint and the midpoint of the segment joining two grid points, normalised by wall length, which must go to zero with resolution for the discrete Laplacian to be consistent. That is what Part I deferred and what the archive could not previously reach.

title: ask.py: the fake agent's final Complete call raises on the pinned fhlmi/fhaviary
description: After gen_answer succeeds, run_fake_agent asks the model to call the Complete tool. fhlmi 1.0.7's LiteLLMModel.select_tool builds a keyword-only _acompletion closure, while fhaviary 0.36.0's ToolSelector.__call__ passes the messages positionally, so it raises TypeError: _acompletion() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given. paperqa catches it, logs 'Trajectory failed.' and marks the run FAIL. The answer and its contexts are already built by then, so ask.py prints the right thing and exits 0, but the traceback is on stderr and the status the session carries is wrong. Either pin an fhlmi that matches fhaviary 0.36.0, or drive search, gather and answer directly instead of through run_fake_agent, which is what the ask() comment describes anyway.
acceptance_criteria: A query prints no traceback and the session status is not FAIL.
notes:
The cause, traced 2026-09-10: fhaviary 0.36.0's ToolSelector.__init__ does partial(acompletion, model_name), binding the model name POSITIONALLY, while fhlmi 1.0.7's LiteLLMModel.select_tool supplies a keyword-only closure, async def _acompletion(**kw). Every select_tool call therefore raises TypeError. The two packages are both pinned, so this is not drift; they simply do not fit.

Fixed by not making the call. ask.py no longer goes through PaperQA's agent_query and its fake agent. gather_and_answer() drives search, gather_evidence and gen_answer in that fixed order, which is what the code always claimed to do, and then calls the complete tool directly with has_successful_answer computed from whether an answer was actually generated. That flag is the entire effect of the fourth call, and it is a fact this process already holds; asking a language model for it cost a round trip, could be wrong, and on these pins could not run at all.

VERIFIED SO FAR, with the generator down: no TypeError, no traceback, exit 0, and the status is reported rather than swallowed. STILL TO VERIFY, and it needs TabbyAPI up: that a successful query ends SUCCESS rather than UNSURE or FAIL, and that its answer and citations match what the old path produced for the Millero question.
close_reason:
Fixed by not making the call at all. ask.py no longer goes through PaperQA's agent_query or its fake agent; gather_and_answer() drives search, gather_evidence and gen_answer in that fixed order and then calls the complete tool directly, with has_successful_answer computed from whether an answer was generated. That flag is the whole effect of the fourth call, and the language model was being asked for a fact this process already holds.

Cause, for the record: fhaviary 0.36.0 binds the completion function's model name positionally via partial(acompletion, model_name), while fhlmi 1.0.7's select_tool supplies a keyword-only closure. Both pinned, so not drift; they do not fit.

Verified against the live server, two queries, exit 0 each: no TypeError, no traceback, no 'Provider List' banner, and no status line, meaning both ended SUCCESS rather than the FAIL every run carried before. title: Two suites define closed_set in Main and one silently overwrites the other
description:
The suite prints, on every run:

  WARNING: Method definition closed_set(Type, Any) in module Main at test/events/runtests.jl:15 overwritten at test/verdicts/runtests.jl:15.

test/runtests.jl includes each suite's entry point into Main, so two suites defining a helper of the same name collide there and the later include wins. Both definitions are the same today, so nothing is currently wrong, which is exactly why it is worth fixing before it is: a change to one suite's helper would silently change the other suite's behaviour, and the only warning is a line nobody reads in a passing run.

The helper is the closed-vocabulary check shared by Verdicts and Events, and more vocabularies are closed the same way (Semantics and TimeSemantics in the fields plan, the dispositions in the system plan), so the collision will grow rather than go away. Either give each suite its own module rather than dropping names into Main, or lift closed_set somewhere both include once.

Boundary: test/runtests.jl; test/events/runtests.jl; test/verdicts/runtests.jl; a shared test helper file if that is the answer.
design: test/runtests.jl, which discovers and includes each suite; test/verdicts/runtests.jl and test/events/runtests.jl, the two definitions
acceptance_criteria: The suite runs with no method-overwritten warning; both vocabulary closure checks still pass with their positive controls firing; a third suite defining a helper of the same name does not silently replace either, demonstrated by a fixture

title: The ulp-ensemble finding says cells where it means vertices
description:
notes/findings/2026-09-11-ulp-ensemble-member-count.md writes, in the section on what the ensemble cannot see, that at a level with 163842 cells the twelve degree-five elements are one part in 13653. 163842 is nvertices(7) = 10*4^7+2. The cell count at that level is ncells(7) = 20*4^7 = 327680. The arithmetic in the finding is internally consistent and its conclusion stands; the noun is wrong.

It matters because the twelve are a property of the VERTICES of a triangle mesh, not of its faces, and decision 0005 makes triangles the cells. A reader following that sentence would look for twelve special cells among 327680 and find nothing. fiddlybits-52v.7.17 caught this while implementing the check and identified them by computed valence instead; verified at level 5, exactly 12 vertices of valence five and 10230 of valence six.

A finding is frozen: it is a dated record of what was measured on its date and is not rewritten to stay current. So this is corrected by a NEW record that supersedes the sentence, naming the original by path, not by editing it.

title: Stencil construction allocates a vector per vertex star and a set per cell
description:
Observed in review of fiddlybits-52v.2.4 at 131c221, alongside the same class of defect fixed for bisection in fiddlybits-52v.2.9. build_vertex_neighbour holds the incident cells of every vertex as a Vector{Int32} per vertex and collects each cell's neighbours through a Set and a sort, so the build allocates far above the tables it produces.

Measured on yggdrasil, Julia 1.12.7, best of three with a collection between runs: building the stencils of level 7 takes 0.164 s and allocates 133.1 MiB against 41.2 MiB of tables; level 6 takes 0.042 s and allocates 32.3 MiB against 10.3 MiB.

The stars are a fixed-valence structure and can be a counted CSR pair sized from the cells table in one pass, and the per-cell neighbour set can be a reused scratch buffer, since the result is sorted and capped at twelve.

This is a build-once cost per level, not an inner loop, which is why it was filed rather than fixed inside the row.

File boundary: src/Mesh/stencils.jl; test/mesh/stencil_valence.jl.
acceptance_criteria: Every assertion already in test/mesh/stencil_valence.jl passes unchanged, including the ordering of vertex_neighbour ascending by cell index with the padding last, since a later row digests these tables; building the stencils of a level allocates within a small multiple of the tables returned, asserted by @allocated against the computed table size
notes: Merged to main at 586cfd2. Suite 351 of 351. Building the stencils of level 7 on yggdrasil, Julia 1.12.7, best of three with a collection between runs: 0.164 s and 133.1 MiB before, 0.050 s and 58.6 MiB after, against 41.2 MiB of tables, so the build went from 3.2 times its tables to 1.4. The suite asserts it stays within twice. The two structural assumptions the change rests on are now refused by name with synthetic positive controls rather than being silent: an edge count above what a closed triangulated surface admits, and a vertex incident on more cells than a bisection level produces. The remaining excess is the edge dictionary and the stars matrix; a hash-free edge numbering through the stars is possible and was not taken, since the numbering convention the tables and the later digest depend on would have to be preserved exactly.

title: The zarr HTML spec sits in references/pdf and is outside the digest bookkeeping
description:
references/pdf/zarr-v3-core-specification.html is the one source in the paper directory that is not a PDF. Two consequences, one now fixed and one not.

Fixed incidentally on 2026-09-10: it had been recorded in the index as ERROR, so it was never actually indexed, and nothing said so. Treating an ERROR entry as stale rather than adopting it put it through on the next build, and it now carries a real hash. PaperQA reads HTML itself rather than through ask.py's parser, which is why it works.

Not fixed: ask.py's staleness bookkeeping globs '*.pdf'. It builds on_disk from PDFs alone, so this file has no entry in text-digests.toml, 737 digests against 738 indexed sources. A change to its content will never be noticed, and --build will never re-read it. It is also outside extract_text.py and the OCR chain for the same reason.

Either widen the glob to the extensions the archive actually holds and give the file a digest of its own bytes, or move it out of references/pdf and record it as a reference of a different kind. The first is smaller; the second is probably more honest, since the directory is named for what it holds.
acceptance_criteria: Every source the index holds has a digest, and a change to any of them is picked up by --build.
close_reason: ask.py now has one definition of what counts as a source, SOURCE_SUFFIXES over pdf, html, htm, txt and md, used by the manifest, the build and the digest bookkeeping alike. The INDEX.md row regex was hardcoded to .pdf too, so the zarr row had been written and silently ignored; relabel has now applied its citation. text_digest takes the source rather than a stem and hashes the extracted text where there is any, the file's own bytes where there is not, because hashing an absent text directory gave every such source the same digest and made all of them permanently unstale. 738 sources on disk, 738 digests recorded, none missing and none out of date; verified that appending a byte to the HTML file changes its digest and that restoring it changes it back.

title: Two dated findings cite OCR pass lists that no longer exist
description:
notes/findings/2026-09-08-ocr-chandra-vs-tesseract.md cites tools/references/ocr_layer_files.txt and tools/references/scanned_native_layer_files.txt as the provenance of its page counts. Those three pass lists were replaced on 2026-09-10 by a single tools/references/pending_ocr.txt, so both paths are now dead.

The finding itself is not wrong. It is a dated record of what was measured on 2026-09-08 and the files existed then, which is why it was left alone rather than rewritten to name a file that did not exist at the time. Git history holds the deleted lists. What is missing is a pointer saying so, and a reader following the path today just finds nothing.

Decide whether a dated finding may carry a later editorial note, or whether the convention is that a dead path in a finding is read through git. Whichever way it goes, it is a convention worth writing down once in docs/practice.md rather than deciding again each time.
acceptance_criteria: docs/practice.md says what happens to a path named in a dated finding when the file moves, and the two references in the 2026-09-08 finding follow it.
close_reason: Wrong question, and mine. A dated finding is a historical record: it says what was measured and what was true on the day it was written. Amending one after the fact to point at a file that did not exist then is an antipattern, not a convention to be chosen. A path that has since moved is resolved through git history, which holds it. No practice note is needed and none should be written.

title: The query-side embedder reloads 15 GB per process to encode one sentence
description:
Measured 2026-09-10. With TabbyAPI resident the card has about 2.5 GiB free, so the 8B embedder runs on the CPU. Cost, measured on its own: 3.7 s to load the model, 0.36 s to encode one query. About 4 s of a 31 s query, nearly all of it the load.

THE CARD IS NOT THE ANSWER, and an earlier version of this row said it was. The arithmetic: the card is 24 GiB, the generator holds 18.3, and the embedder takes 17.6 at fp16. They do not both fit, and it makes no difference who loads it. That TabbyAPI lists Qwen3-Embedding-8B among its models means only that the file is in the models directory; listing is not residency. The reranker is a different case and already sits on the card, because it is 1.2 GB.

What is actually wrong is the reload, not the device. A query encodes ONE short string, 0.36 s of work, and pays 3.7 s to bring up a 15 GB model to do it. A build is the opposite case and is already handled: it embeds the whole archive in one process, and it runs when the card is free.

So the options are about residency, not hardware:
- Hold the embedder in a process that outlives one query: a small local endpoint, or ask.py as a session rather than a command. Takes the per-query cost to about 0.4 s.
- Quantise it. int8 is roughly 8 GiB and nf4 roughly 4.5; neither fits beside the generator either, but both make the load cheaper. Retrieval quality unmeasured, and the 2026-09-08 A/B chose this model on exactly the queries a smaller or coarser model got wrong.
- Accept 4 s. It is 13 percent of a query and the rest is the generator.

Worth saying plainly: this is a small cost on a path that is already dominated by the language model, which is why the priority is down from 2 to 3.
acceptance_criteria: A single query against a live served generator returns in seconds, not minutes, with the device it used stated.
notes: Superseded my first reading of this, which blamed the embedder from the wall-clock alone without splitting the phases.
